From Euclidean space to a manifold

A normal law has several coordinate descriptions: mean and standard deviation, mean and variance, natural parameters, or expected sufficient statistics. A change of coordinates changes the numbers used to describe a perturbation of the law. It should preserve the perturbation itself and its statistical size.

This note develops the geometry needed to make that distinction precise. We construct tangent vectors, use Fisher information to measure them, and define connections that differentiate and transport them. The family N(μ,σ2)N(\mu,\sigma^2)N(μ,σ2) provides explicit calculations throughout. It also exhibits a distinction that matters later: its Fisher metric has negative Riemannian curvature, while its exponential and mixture connections are flat.

A running example: normal location and scale¶

Let MMM be the set of laws N(μ,σ2)N(\mu,\sigma^2)N(μ,σ2) with μ∈R\mu\in\mathbb Rμ∈R and σ>0\sigma>0σ>0. Relative to Lebesgue measure on R\mathbb RR,

pξ(x)=12π σexp⁡ ⁣(−(x−μ)22σ2),ξ=(μ,σ)T.p_\xi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \qquad \xi=(\mu,\sigma)^{\mathsf T}.pξ​(x)=2π​σ1​exp(−2σ2(x−μ)2​),ξ=(μ,σ)T.
(1)

The sample space is one-dimensional, but the family of laws is two-dimensional. The mean and variance determine each law uniquely. We exclude σ=0\sigma=0σ=0, whose point mass is outside this density model.

What makes this a manifold¶

A smooth ddd-manifold is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space covered by coordinate neighborhoods, each homeomorphic to an open subset of Rd\mathbb R^dRd, with smooth transition maps between these charts. A chart assigns coordinates to points; its inverse interprets coordinate values as points of the manifold. The normal family obtains such a structure from its bijection with R×(0,∞)\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)R×(0,∞), and the other charts above are smoothly compatible with it.

A general parameterized statistical model needs more care. Parameters may repeat the same law, and even an injective parameterization can have a vanishing first derivative at a point. We work on regular regions where the model is locally identifiable and the Fisher matrix is smooth and positive definite. The normal calculation below verifies that condition. A statistical manifold need not be presented as a curved surface inside a Euclidean space.

Tangent vectors, functions, and differentials¶

Curves define tangent vectors¶

Fix q∈Mq\in Mq∈M and a chart ξ\xiξ containing it. Two smooth curves c1,c2c_1,c_2c1​,c2​ through qqq at r=0r=0r=0 are equivalent when

ddrξi(c1(r))∣r=0=ddrξi(c2(r))∣r=0for every i.\left.\frac{d}{dr}\xi^i(c_1(r))\right|_{r=0} = \left.\frac{d}{dr}\xi^i(c_2(r))\right|_{r=0} \quad\text{for every }i.drd​ξi(c1​(r))∣∣​r=0​=drd​ξi(c2​(r))∣∣​r=0​for every i.
(5)

The chain rule makes this equivalence independent of the chart. A tangent vector is an equivalence class v=[c]v=[c]v=[c] of such curves. Its components are vi=(ξi∘c)′(0)v^i=(\xi^i\circ c)'(0)vi=(ξi∘c)′(0). Every column of ddd real numbers is realized by a coordinate line ξ(c(r))=ξ(q)+rv\xi(c(r))=\xi(q)+rvξ(c(r))=ξ(q)+rv for sufficiently small rrr. These components give the set of classes a ddd-dimensional vector-space structure, called TqMT_qMTq​M; coordinate changes act linearly on that space.

For normals, v=vμ∂μ+vσ∂σv=v^\mu\partial_\mu+v^\sigma\partial_\sigmav=vμ∂μ​+vσ∂σ​ is represented by (μ(r),σ(r))=(μ+rvμ,σ+rvσ)(\mu(r),\sigma(r))=(\mu+rv^\mu,\sigma+rv^\sigma)(μ(r),σ(r))=(μ+rvμ,σ+rvσ) near r=0r=0r=0. The coordinates of a law and the components of a tangent vector have different roles: one specifies a distribution; the other specifies rates of change at that distribution.

The equivalent definition by derivations¶

A derivation at qqq is an R\mathbb RR-linear map A:C∞(M)→RA:C^\infty(M)\to\mathbb RA:C∞(M)→R satisfying the pointwise Leibniz rule

A(FH)=F(q)A(H)+H(q)A(F).A(FH)=F(q)A(H)+H(q)A(F).A(FH)=F(q)A(H)+H(q)A(F).
(6)

It depends only on functions near qqq. Indeed, if FFF vanishes near qqq, choose a smooth cutoff equal to one at qqq and supported where F=0F=0F=0; applying the product rule to their zero product gives A(F)=0A(F)=0A(F)=0. Thus we can also work with germs of smooth functions at qqq, and apply AAA to local coordinate functions.

A curve class defines such a derivation by

v[F]=ddrF(c(r))∣r=0=vi∂iF(q),∂i∣q[F]=∂(F∘ξ−1)∂ξi∣ξ(q).v[F]=\left.\frac{d}{dr}F(c(r))\right|_{r=0} =v^i\partial_iF(q),\qquad \partial_i\big|_q[F] =\left.\frac{\partial(F\circ\xi^{-1})}{\partial\xi^i}\right|_{\xi(q)}.v[F]=drd​F(c(r))∣∣​r=0​=vi∂i​F(q),∂i​∣∣​q​[F]=∂ξi∂(F∘ξ−1)​∣∣​ξ(q)​.
(7)

F(y)−F(q)=(ξi(y)−ξi(q))Hi(y),Hi(q)=∂iF(q).F(y)-F(q)=(\xi^i(y)-\xi^i(q))H_i(y),\qquad H_i(q)=\partial_iF(q).F(y)−F(q)=(ξi(y)−ξi(q))Hi​(y),Hi​(q)=∂i​F(q).
(8)

Applying its product rule to this expansion gives A(F)=A(ξi)∂iF(q)A(F)=A(\xi^i)\partial_iF(q)A(F)=A(ξi)∂i​F(q). Metrics and Fisher information¶

A metric is more than a parameter norm¶

A Riemannian metric ggg assigns a smooth positive definite symmetric bilinear form gqg_qgq​ to every tangent space. Its components are gij=g(∂i,∂j)g_{ij}=g(\partial_i,\partial_j)gij​=g(∂i​,∂j​). Substituting vi=Biav′av^i=B^i{}_a v'^avi=Bia​v′a and wj=Bjbw′bw^j=B^j{}_b w'^bwj=Bjb​w′b gives

gab′(ϕ)=BiaBjbgij(ξ),Gϕ(ϕ)=BTGξ(ξ)B=Df(ξ)−TGξ(ξ)Df(ξ)−1,ϕ=f(ξ).\begin{aligned} g'_{ab}(\phi)&=B^i{}_a B^j{}_b g_{ij}(\xi),\\ G_\phi(\phi)&=B^{\mathsf T}G_\xi(\xi)B =Df(\xi)^{-\mathsf T}G_\xi(\xi)Df(\xi)^{-1}, \qquad \phi=f(\xi). \end{aligned}gab′​(ϕ)Gϕ​(ϕ)​=Bia​Bjb​gij​(ξ),=BTGξ​(ξ)B=Df(ξ)−TGξ​(ξ)Df(ξ)−1,ϕ=f(ξ).​
(14)

Every Riemannian metric has this covariance. It does not by itself select Fisher information. Even a Euclidean metric acquires nonconstant coefficients in nonlinear coordinates. On an angular sector of the Euclidean plane, write x=ρcos⁡φx=\rho\cos\varphix=ρcosφ, y=ρsin⁡φy=\rho\sin\varphiy=ρsinφ, with radius ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0. Then

ds2=dx2+dy2=dρ2+ρ2dφ2.ds^2=dx^2+dy^2=d\rho^2+\rho^2d\varphi^2.ds2=dx2+dy2=dρ2+ρ2dφ2.
(15)

Thus nonconstant metric coefficients alone do not establish curvature.

For normals, choosing dμ2+dσ2d\mu^2+d\sigma^2dμ2+dσ2 in the scale chart and choosing dμ2+dτ2d\mu^2+d\tau^2dμ2+dτ2 afresh in the variance chart gives incompatible metrics:

dμ2+dτ2=dμ2+4σ2dσ2.d\mu^2+d\tau^2=d\mu^2+4\sigma^2d\sigma^2.dμ2+dτ2=dμ2+4σ2dσ2.
(16)

At σ=2\sigma=2σ=2, the same unit scale velocity has squared lengths 1 and 16. A Euclidean metric chosen in one chart is legitimate, but must then be transformed by (14). A statistical principle is needed to choose a metric without privileging that chart.

For a piecewise smooth curve c:[a,b]→Mc:[a,b]\to Mc:[a,b]→M, the metric determines length and intrinsic distance by

Lg(c)=∫abgij(ξ(c(r)))ξ˙iξ˙j dr,dg(q0,q1)=inf⁡c:q0→q1Lg(c).L_g(c)=\int_a^b\sqrt{g_{ij}(\xi(c(r)))\dot\xi^i\dot\xi^j}\,dr, \qquad d_g(q_0,q_1)=\inf_{c:q_0\to q_1}L_g(c).Lg​(c)=∫ab​gij​(ξ(c(r)))ξ˙​iξ˙​j​dr,dg​(q0​,q1​)=c:q0​→q1​inf​Lg​(c).
(17)

The infimum is over curves in the specified manifold. Restricting to a subfamily can increase this distance.

Scores measure changes in the law¶

For a general model, assume positive densities on a common support relative to a fixed measure ν\nuν. Assume smooth parameter dependence, square-integrable scores, and local integrable bounds allowing differentiation of the normalizer and the expectations used below. We will specify the additional Taylor and third-moment assumptions where they are needed.

Differentiating the density and its normalization gives

∂ipξ=pξsi,Eξ[si]=0,ddrℓξ(c(r))(x)∣r=0=si(x)vi.\partial_i p_\xi=p_\xi s_i,\qquad \mathbb E_\xi[s_i]=0,\qquad \left.\frac{d}{dr}\ell_{\xi(c(r))}(x)\right|_{r=0}=s_i(x)v^i.∂i​pξ​=pξ​si​,Eξ​[si​]=0,drd​ℓξ(c(r))​(x)∣∣​r=0​=si​(x)vi.
(18)

The Fisher metric per observation is

gξ(v,w)=Eξ[(sivi)(sjwj)],gij(ξ)=Eξ[sisj],I(ξ)=Eξ[sξsξT].\begin{aligned} g_\xi(v,w)&=\mathbb E_\xi[(s_i v^i)(s_j w^j)],\\ g_{ij}(\xi)&=\mathbb E_\xi[s_i s_j],\qquad I(\xi)=\mathbb E_\xi[s_\xi s_\xi^{\mathsf T}]. \end{aligned}gξ​(v,w)gij​(ξ)​=Eξ​[(si​vi)(sj​wj)],=Eξ​[si​sj​],I(ξ)=Eξ​[sξ​sξT​].​
(19)

It is positive semidefinite; our regularity assumption requires positive definiteness. A zero length direction would have zero first-order density change almost everywhere. Under reparameterization the score obeys sa′=Biasis'_a=B^i{}_a s_isa′​=Bia​si​, so its covariance obeys exactly the metric transformation law. Invertible, parameter-independent changes of the observed variable also preserve Fisher information: their density Jacobian contributes a term to the log density whose parameter derivative is zero.

Computing the normal metric¶

Set Z=(X−μ)/σ∼N(0,1)Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma\sim N(0,1)Z=(X−μ)/σ∼N(0,1). Differentiating (1),

sμ=X−μσ2=Zσ,sσ=−1σ+(X−μ)2σ3=Z2−1σ.s_\mu=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma^2}=\frac Z\sigma, \qquad s_\sigma=-\frac1\sigma+\frac{(X-\mu)^2}{\sigma^3} =\frac{Z^2-1}{\sigma}.sμ​=σ2X−μ​=σZ​,sσ​=−σ1​+σ3(X−μ)2​=σZ2−1​.
(20)

The subscripts here denote covector components, not differentiation of an already defined score. Odd standard-normal moments vanish, and integration by parts gives E[Z2k]=(2k−1)E[Z2k−2]\mathbb E[Z^{2k}]=(2k-1)\mathbb E[Z^{2k-2}]E[Z2k]=(2k−1)E[Z2k−2]. Natural and expectation coordinates¶

In natural coordinates sθ=t−ηs_\theta=t-\etasθ​=t−η, so differentiating the normalizer in (2) gives the matrix identities

Why Fisher information is distinguished¶

Coordinate covariance is required of every metric. Fisher information has additional properties concerning statistical distinguishability and the loss of observations. We prove the local KL and monotonicity statements below; the uniqueness theorem is cited with its finite-space hypotheses.

The Hessian of KL at the diagonal¶

Use the direction D(pξ∥pζ)=Eξ[ℓξ−ℓζ]D(p_\xi\|p_\zeta)=\mathbb E_\xi[\ell_\xi-\ell_\zeta]D(pξ​∥pζ​)=Eξ​[ℓξ​−ℓζ​], holding the first law fixed. Differentiating normalization twice yields

0=Eξ[∂i∂jℓξ+sisj],Eξ[∂i∂jℓξ]=−gij.0=\mathbb E_\xi[\partial_i\partial_j\ell_\xi+s_i s_j], \qquad \mathbb E_\xi[\partial_i\partial_j\ell_\xi]=-g_{ij}.0=Eξ​[∂i​∂j​ℓξ​+si​sj​],Eξ​[∂i​∂j​ℓξ​]=−gij​.
(24)

Assume in addition that ζ↦Eξ[ℓζ]\zeta\mapsto\mathbb E_\xi[\ell_\zeta]ζ↦Eξ​[ℓζ​] has a third-order Taylor remainder bounded by a constant times ∥ζ−ξ∥3\lVert\zeta-\xi\rVert^3∥ζ−ξ∥3 locally. For example, locally bounded integrable third derivatives of the log density under PξP_\xiPξ​ suffice. Taylor expansion then gives

D(pξ∥pξ+δξ)=12gij(ξ) δξiδξj+O(∥δξ∥3).D(p_\xi\|p_{\xi+\delta\xi}) =\frac12 g_{ij}(\xi)\,\delta\xi^i\delta\xi^j +O(\lVert\delta\xi\rVert^3).D(pξ​∥pξ+δξ​)=21​gij​(ξ)δξiδξj+O(∥δξ∥3).
(25)

The zero expected score removes the linear term. The Hessian in the second argument at equality is therefore gijg_{ij}gij​; because the first derivative vanishes there, this Hessian transforms tensorially. With only a second-order Taylor expansion, the remainder is o(∥δξ∥2)o(\lVert\delta\xi\rVert^2)o(∥δξ∥2), as in the Fisher-versus-L2L^2L2 note. Finite KL remains asymmetric and is not half the squared Fisher–Rao distance.

For normals the exact expression is

D ⁣(N(μ,σ2)∥N(μ~,σ~2))=log⁡σ~σ−12+σ2+(μ−μ~)22σ~2.D\!\left(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\middle\|N(\widetilde\mu,\widetilde\sigma^2)\right) =\log\frac{\widetilde\sigma}{\sigma}-\frac12 +\frac{\sigma^2+(\mu-\widetilde\mu)^2}{2\widetilde\sigma^2}.D(N(μ,σ2)∥∥​N(μ​,σ2))=logσσ​−21​+2σ2σ2+(μ−μ​)2​.

Putting (μ~,σ~)=(μ+εa,σ+εb)(\widetilde\mu,\widetilde\sigma) =(\mu+\varepsilon a,\sigma+\varepsilon b)(μ​,σ)=(μ+εa,σ+εb) at a fixed σ>0\sigma>0σ>0 gives ε2(a2+2b2)/(2σ2)+O(ε3)\varepsilon^2(a^2+2b^2)/(2\sigma^2)+O(\varepsilon^3)ε2(a2+2b2)/(2σ2)+O(ε3), in agreement with (21).

Coarse-graining, monotonicity, and sufficiency¶

Let an observation XXX pass through a parameter-independent Markov kernel K(dy∣x)K(dy\mid x)K(dy∣x), giving YYY. A deterministic statistic Y=S(X)Y=S(X)Y=S(X) is a special case. Assume the transformed model admits densities and differentiation under the kernel integral, and that the original scores are square integrable. Denote the two score covectors by siXs^X_isiX​ and siYs^Y_isiY​, and their component columns by sξXs^X_\xisξX​ and sξYs^Y_\xisξY​. Differentiating the marginal density of YYY gives

siY(Y)=Eξ[siX(X)∣Y].s^Y_i(Y)=\mathbb E_\xi[s^X_i(X)\mid Y].siY​(Y)=Eξ​[siX​(X)∣Y].
(27)

Thus the new directional score is the conditional expectation of the old one. The conditional-variance identity proves information monotonicity:

gξX(v,v)−gξY(v,v)=Eξ ⁣[Var⁡ξ(visiX(X)∣Y)]≥0,IX(ξ)−IY(ξ)=Eξ[Cov⁡ξ(sξX∣Y)]⪰0.\begin{aligned} g^X_\xi(v,v)-g^Y_\xi(v,v) &=\mathbb E_\xi\!\left[ \operatorname{Var}_\xi(v^i s^X_i(X)\mid Y)\right]\geq0,\\ I_X(\xi)-I_Y(\xi) &=\mathbb E_\xi[\operatorname{Cov}_\xi(s^X_\xi\mid Y)]\succeq0. \end{aligned}gξX​(v,v)−gξY​(v,v)IX​(ξ)−IY​(ξ)​=Eξ​[Varξ​(visiX​(X)∣Y)]≥0,=Eξ​[Covξ​(sξX​∣Y)]⪰0.​
(28)

The superscripts X,YX,YX,Y identify experiments; they are not tensor indices. The output information can be singular. Equality for one vector at one parameter means exactly that its directional score is determined by YYY almost surely. Equality of the matrices at that parameter means this for every score component. This is a statement about first-order information at that point.

A statistic is sufficient for the family if the conditional distribution of XXX given the statistic can be chosen independently of the parameter. Equivalently in the regular dominated setting, the density factors into a parameter-dependent function of the statistic and a parameter-independent factor. Its scores are functions of the statistic, so sufficiency implies equality of Fisher information throughout the family.

For a precise converse, take a finite sample space with strictly positive smooth probabilities on a connected open parameter domain, and a fixed statistic SSS. Equality of Fisher information at every parameter is then equivalent to sufficiency. To prove the converse, equality in (28) gives, for every outcome,

∂ilog⁡Pξ(X=x∣S(X)=S(x))=siX(x)−siS(S(x))=0.\partial_i\log P_\xi(X=x\mid S(X)=S(x)) =s^X_i(x)-s^S_i(S(x))=0.∂i​logPξ​(X=x∣S(X)=S(x))=siX​(x)−siS​(S(x))=0.
(29)

Connectedness makes each conditional probability constant in the parameter, which proves sufficiency. Equality at one parameter, or in one direction, is insufficient for this conclusion. Extensions beyond this finite positive setting need corresponding regularity assumptions; see Ay, Jost, Lê, and Schwachhöfer on sufficient statistics.

The normal family illustrates both preservation and loss. For independent observations X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​, the statistic S=(∑aXa,∑aXa2)S=(\sum_a X_a,\sum_a X_a^2)S=(∑a​Xa​,∑a​Xa2​) is sufficient by the factorization in (2). Its information equals that of the full sample, namely nI(ξ)nI(\xi)nI(ξ): independent zero-mean scores add and their cross-covariances vanish. By contrast, retaining only Y=1{X>0}Y=\mathbf 1_{\{X>0\}}Y=1{X>0}​ gives a Bernoulli probability q=Φ(μ/σ)q=\Phi(\mu/\sigma)q=Φ(μ/σ), where Φ\PhiΦ is the standard-normal cdf. At μ=0\mu=0μ=0, ∂μq=1/(2πσ)\partial_\mu q=1/(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma)∂μ​q=1/(2π​σ) and ∂σq=0\partial_\sigma q=0∂σ​q=0, so

IY(0,σ)=(2/(πσ2)000).I_Y(0,\sigma)=\begin{pmatrix}2/(\pi\sigma^2)&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.IY​(0,σ)=(2/(πσ2)0​00​).
(30)

The sign loses all local scale information and retains only a fraction 2/π2/\pi2/π of the location information there.

Čencov’s finite-space uniqueness theorem¶

The theorem concerns a compatible choice of metrics on all finite probability simplices, not an arbitrary metric on one fixed normal family. Let

Δn−1∘={p∈Rn:p(a)>0, ∑a=1np(a)=1},TpΔn−1∘={u∈Rn:∑a=1nu(a)=0}.\Delta_{n-1}^{\circ} =\left\{p\in\mathbb R^n:p(a)>0,\ \sum_{a=1}^n p(a)=1\right\}, \qquad T_p\Delta_{n-1}^{\circ} =\left\{u\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_{a=1}^n u(a)=0\right\}.Δn−1∘​={p∈Rn:p(a)>0, a=1∑n​p(a)=1},Tp​Δn−1∘​={u∈Rn:a=1∑n​u(a)=0}.
(31)

A Markov map is a stochastic linear map (Kp)(b)=∑aK(b∣a)p(a)(Kp)(b)=\sum_a K(b\mid a)p(a)(Kp)(b)=∑a​K(b∣a)p(a). A congruent Markov embedding has a Markov left inverse LLL with LK=idLK=\mathrm{id}LK=id and maps the interior into the interior. It splits each input outcome into a disjoint block of output outcomes with fixed conditional probabilities; the block label recovers the input. Such a splitting preserves the statistical experiment.

Čencov’s theorem states that if smooth Riemannian metrics h(n)h^{(n)}h(n) on Δn−1∘\Delta_{n-1}^{\circ}Δn−1∘​, for every n≥2n\geq2n≥2, make every congruent Markov embedding an isometry, then there is a single constant c>0c>0c>0, independent of nnn and ppp, such that

hp(n)(u,w)=c∑a=1nu(a)w(a)p(a).h^{(n)}_p(u,w)=c\sum_{a=1}^n\frac{u(a)w(a)}{p(a)}.hp(n)​(u,w)=ca=1∑n​p(a)u(a)w(a)​.
(32)

Conversely, these metrics have that invariance. We cite this classification, not prove it: see Čencov’s Statistical Decision Rules and Optimal Inference (1982) and the explicit finite-simplex formulation in Theorem 2 of Montúfar, Rauh, and Ay (2014).

Pulling (32) back along a regular finite statistical model, with u(a)=∂ipξ(a)vi=pξ(a)si(a)viu(a)=\partial_i p_\xi(a)v^i=p_\xi(a)s_i(a)v^iu(a)=∂i​pξ​(a)vi=pξ​(a)si​(a)vi, gives cgξ(v,w)cg_\xi(v,w)cgξ​(v,w). We choose c=1c=1c=1 for information per observation. General Markov maps are contractions by (28), whereas sufficient transformations preserve information. Requiring invariance under every Markov map would be wrong: a kernel can discard the observation completely. Equivalently, demanding monotonicity for a family of metrics under all such maps forces the isometries above, since KKK and its Markov left inverse give opposite inequalities.

For general sample spaces, Ay–Jost–Lê–Schwachhöfer (2017) develop invariance and uniqueness results for suitable integrable models and continuous local tensor fields. A different extension by Bauer–Bruveris–Michor (2016) characterizes the Fisher metric among smooth weak Riemannian metrics invariant under observation-space diffeomorphisms on smooth positive probability densities over a closed manifold of dimension greater than one. Neither statement is an unrestricted uniqueness theorem for every continuous or singular statistical model; in particular, that latter theorem does not directly cover densities on R\mathbb RR.

Density L2L^2L2 and square-root densities¶

The raw density metric, when finite, gijraw=∫(∂ip)(∂jp) dνg^{\mathrm{raw}}_{ij}=\int(\partial_i p)(\partial_j p)\,d\nugijraw​=∫(∂i​p)(∂j​p)dν, also transforms correctly under parameter changes. It depends on the reference measure and the measurement coordinate: for Lebesgue densities and Y=aXY=aXY=aX, a>0a>0a>0, ∫(pY−qY)2 dy=a−1∫(pX−qX)2 dx\int(p_Y-q_Y)^2\,dy=a^{-1}\int(p_X-q_X)^2\,dx∫(pY​−qY​)2dy=a−1∫(pX​−qX​)2dx. It therefore differs from Fisher geometry even though both constructions are covariant under reparameterization.

Assuming differentiability into L2(ν)L^2(\nu)L2(ν), the map p↦2pp\mapsto2\sqrt pp↦2p​ has derivative ∂i(2p)=p si\partial_i(2\sqrt p)=\sqrt p\,s_i∂i​(2p​)=p​si​. Its pullback of the L2L^2L2 inner product is exactly gijg_{ij}gij​. With H2(p,q)=12∫(p−q)2 dνH^2(p,q)=\tfrac12\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\nuH2(p,q)=21​∫(p​−q​)2dν, this gives H2(pξ,pξ+δξ)=18gijδξiδξj+o(∥δξ∥2)H^2(p_\xi,p_{\xi+\delta\xi})=\tfrac18g_{ij}\delta\xi^i\delta\xi^j +o(\lVert\delta\xi\rVert^2)H2(pξ​,pξ+δξ​)=81​gij​δξiδξj+o(∥δξ∥2). The Fisher-versus-L2L^2L2 note explains the distinct roles of parameter norms, scores in L2(Pξ)L^2(P_\xi)L2(Pξ​), and densities in L2(ν)L^2(\nu)L2(ν). A square-root embedding preserves tangent lengths; the distance between two normals still minimizes paths within the normal family, rather than over the whole sphere of square-root densities.

Connections differentiate vector fields¶

The ordinary derivative of vector components depends on the chosen chart. For example, a field with constant scale component has variance component 2σ2\sigma2σ times as large, which changes along a scale curve. A connection supplies the correction that makes differentiation independent of coordinates. It is extra geometric structure; a metric singles out one connection only when we impose the conditions below.

Axioms and Christoffel symbols¶

An affine connection on MMM is an R\mathbb RR-bilinear operation (U,V)↦∇UV(U,V)\mapsto\nabla_UV(U,V)↦∇U​V on smooth vector fields satisfying, for every smooth function aaa,

∇aUV=a∇UV,∇U(aV)=U[a]V+a∇UV.\nabla_{aU}V=a\nabla_UV,\qquad \nabla_U(aV)=U[a]V+a\nabla_UV.∇aU​V=a∇U​V,∇U​(aV)=U[a]V+a∇U​V.
(33)

Thus the lower argument UUU is linear over functions; in the differentiated argument VVV, the Leibniz term is essential. At a point, ∇UV\nabla_UV∇U​V depends only on the value of UUU and on the first-order behavior of VVV nearby.

Define the Christoffel symbols in a coordinate basis by

∇∂i∂j=Γijk∂k.\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\Gamma_{ij}^k\partial_k.∇∂i​​∂j​=Γijk​∂k​.
(34)

Expanding U=Ui∂iU=U^i\partial_iU=Ui∂i​ and V=Vj∂jV=V^j\partial_jV=Vj∂j​ with the axioms gives

∇UV=Ui(∂iVk+ΓijkVj)∂k.\nabla_UV=U^i\bigl(\partial_iV^k+\Gamma_{ij}^kV^j\bigr)\partial_k.∇U​V=Ui(∂i​Vk+Γijk​Vj)∂k​.
(35)

The second term accounts for the change of the coordinate basis under the connection. Prescribing smooth Γijk\Gamma_{ij}^kΓijk​ defines a connection on a chart; prescriptions on overlapping charts must satisfy the next law.

Why Christoffel symbols are not a tensor¶

Use ϕ=f(ξ)\phi=f(\xi)ϕ=f(ξ), Aai=∂ϕa/∂ξiA^a{}_i=\partial\phi^a/\partial\xi^iAai​=∂ϕa/∂ξi, and Bia=∂ξi/∂ϕaB^i{}_a=\partial\xi^i/\partial\phi^aBia​=∂ξi/∂ϕa as before. Apply the connection axioms to ∇Bia∂i(Bjb∂j)\nabla_{B^i{}_a\partial_i}(B^j{}_b\partial_j)∇Bia​∂i​​(Bjb​∂j​) to obtain

Γ′abc=AckBiaBjbΓijk+Ack∂2ξk∂ϕa∂ϕb.\Gamma'{}^c_{ab} =A^c{}_k B^i{}_a B^j{}_b\Gamma_{ij}^k +A^c{}_k\frac{\partial^2\xi^k}{\partial\phi^a\partial\phi^b}.Γ′abc​=Ack​Bia​Bjb​Γijk​+Ack​∂ϕa∂ϕb∂2ξk​.
(36)

A (1,2)(1,2)(1,2)-tensor has only the first term. The inhomogeneous second derivative is why coefficients that vanish in one chart need not vanish in another. For example, take the connection with Γijk=0\Gamma_{ij}^k=0Γijk​=0 in the normal location-scale chart. In the variance chart, σ=τ\sigma=\sqrt\tauσ=τ​, so it has

Γ′τττ=2σd2τdτ2=−12τ.\Gamma'{}^{\tau}_{\tau\tau} =2\sigma\frac{d^2\sqrt\tau}{d\tau^2}=-\frac1{2\tau}.Γ′τττ​=2σdτ2d2τ​​=−2τ1​.
(37)

This is a coordinate-flat connection chosen on the parameter domain; it is not yet the Fisher Levi-Civita connection. The example isolates the effect of the second term in (36).

The difference of two connections is a (1,2)(1,2)(1,2)-tensor: their inhomogeneous terms cancel. Equivalently, the Leibniz terms cancel in ∇UV−∇~UV\nabla_UV-\widetilde\nabla_UV∇U​V−∇U​V, leaving an expression linear over functions in both UUU and VVV. We will use this fact to compare statistical connections.

Along a curve: parallel transport and geodesics¶

For a curve c(r)c(r)c(r), let V(r)=Vk(r)∂k∣c(r)V(r)=V^k(r)\partial_k|_{c(r)}V(r)=Vk(r)∂k​∣c(r)​ be a vector field along the curve. It need not extend to a single vector field on all of MMM. Its covariant derivative is

DVdr:=∇c˙V=(dVkdr+Γijk(ξ(c(r)))ξ˙iVj)∂k.\frac{DV}{dr}:=\nabla_{\dot c}V =\left(\frac{dV^k}{dr} +\Gamma_{ij}^k(\xi(c(r)))\dot\xi^i V^j\right)\partial_k.drDV​:=∇c˙​V=(drdVk​+Γijk​(ξ(c(r)))ξ˙​iVj)∂k​.
(38)

The transformation law makes this independent of coordinates. A field is parallel when DV/dr=0DV/dr=0DV/dr=0. Given an initial vector, this linear ODE has a unique solution along a smooth curve on a compact parameter interval. It defines a linear isomorphism between the endpoint tangent spaces, called parallel transport. Reversing the curve gives its inverse. Transport generally depends on the path, not just its endpoints.

An affinely parameterized geodesic has parallel velocity:

∇c˙c˙=0,ξ¨k+Γijkξ˙iξ˙j=0.\nabla_{\dot c}\dot c=0, \qquad \ddot\xi^k+\Gamma_{ij}^k\dot\xi^i\dot\xi^j=0.∇c˙​c˙=0,ξ¨​k+Γijk​ξ˙​iξ˙​j=0.
(39)

An arbitrary nonlinear reparameterization need not preserve this equation; affine changes of the parameter do. A connection defines geodesics without requiring a metric or a length-minimization interpretation.

Torsion, compatibility, and the Levi-Civita connection¶

The Lie bracket is the vector field [U,V][F]=U[V[F]]−V[U[F]][U,V][F]=U[V[F]]-V[U[F]][U,V][F]=U[V[F]]−V[U[F]]. In coordinates, [U,V]k=Ui∂iVk−Vi∂iUk[U,V]^k=U^i\partial_iV^k-V^i\partial_iU^k[U,V]k=Ui∂i​Vk−Vi∂i​Uk. The torsion of a connection is

T(U,V)=∇UV−∇VU−[U,V],T(∂i,∂j)=(Γijk−Γjik)∂k.T(U,V)=\nabla_UV-\nabla_VU-[U,V],\qquad T(\partial_i,\partial_j) =(\Gamma_{ij}^k-\Gamma_{ji}^k)\partial_k.T(U,V)=∇U​V−∇V​U−[U,V],T(∂i​,∂j​)=(Γijk​−Γjik​)∂k​.
(40)

It is a tensor. A connection is torsion-free exactly when its lower Christoffel indices are symmetric in a coordinate basis.

A connection is metric-compatible, written ∇g=0\nabla g=0∇g=0, when

U[g(V,W)]=g(∇UV,W)+g(V,∇UW).U[g(V,W)]=g(\nabla_UV,W)+g(V,\nabla_UW).U[g(V,W)]=g(∇U​V,W)+g(V,∇U​W).
(41)

Equivalently, ∂igjk=Γijℓgℓk+Γikℓgjℓ\partial_i g_{jk}=\Gamma_{ij}^{\ell}g_{\ell k} +\Gamma_{ik}^{\ell}g_{j\ell}∂i​gjk​=Γijℓ​gℓk​+Γikℓ​gjℓ​. Along a curve this product rule shows that parallel transport preserves inner products. In particular, a geodesic for a metric-compatible connection has constant speed.

The Levi-Civita connection ∇LC\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}∇LC is the unique connection that is both torsion-free and compatible with ggg. The identity that determines it is the Koszul formula:

2g(∇ULCV,W)=U[g(V,W)]+V[g(W,U)]−W[g(U,V)]+g([U,V],W)−g([V,W],U)+g([W,U],V).\begin{aligned} 2g(\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}_UV,W) ={}&U[g(V,W)]+V[g(W,U)]-W[g(U,V)]\\ &+g([U,V],W)-g([V,W],U)+g([W,U],V). \end{aligned}2g(∇ULC​V,W)=​U[g(V,W)]+V[g(W,U)]−W[g(U,V)]+g([U,V],W)−g([V,W],U)+g([W,U],V).​
(42)

To see why this determines the connection, write the compatibility identity for the three cyclic choices of U,V,WU,V,WU,V,W, add the first two and subtract the third, and replace ∇UV−∇VU\nabla_UV-\nabla_VU∇U​V−∇V​U by [U,V][U,V][U,V]. This gives (42). Nondegeneracy of ggg then uniquely determines ∇ULCV\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}_UV∇ULC​V. For existence, the right side is linear over functions in WWW, so it defines a vector field by nondegeneracy of ggg. The product rule gives the connection axioms; subtracting the expression with U,VU,VU,V exchanged gives torsion-freeness, and adding the expressions with V,WV,WV,W exchanged gives metric compatibility. In a coordinate basis the brackets vanish, yielding the computable formula

Γij(0)k=12gkℓ(∂igjℓ+∂jgiℓ−∂ℓgij).\Gamma^{(0)k}_{ij} =\frac12g^{k\ell} \left(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_j g_{i\ell} -\partial_\ell g_{ij}\right).Γij(0)k​=21​gkℓ(∂i​gjℓ​+∂j​giℓ​−∂ℓ​gij​).
(43)

We write (0)(0)(0) for Levi-Civita because it will be the α=0\alpha=0α=0 statistical connection. We use the standard Riemannian result that its geodesics minimize length on sufficiently short segments. It does not say every geodesic segment is globally minimizing on every manifold. For background on this result and the connection framework, see §2 of Nielsen’s 2020 introduction.

Levi-Civita geometry of the normal family¶

Substituting (21) into (43) gives exactly these nonzero coefficients:

(45)

Thus a vector transported from scale σ0\sigma_0σ0​ to scale σ1\sigma_1σ1​ has components multiplied by σ1/σ0\sigma_1/\sigma_0σ1​/σ0​. Its Fisher squared length ((Vμ)2+2(Vσ)2)/σ2( (V^\mu)^2+2(V^\sigma)^2 )/\sigma^2((Vμ)2+2(Vσ)2)/σ2 stays fixed. Constant coordinate components would not give parallel transport along this curve.

Make the local coordinate substitution μ=2 u\mu=\sqrt2\,uμ=2​u. Then

ds2=2du2+dσ2σ2,σ>0.ds^2=2\frac{du^2+d\sigma^2}{\sigma^2},\qquad \sigma>0.ds2=2σ2du2+dσ2​,σ>0.

The upper-half-plane distance satisfies cosh⁡dH=1+((u1−u0)2+(σ1−σ0)2)/(2σ0σ1)\cosh d_H=1+((u_1-u_0)^2+(\sigma_1-\sigma_0)^2)/(2\sigma_0\sigma_1)coshdH​=1+((u1​−u0​)2+(σ1​−σ0​)2)/(2σ0​σ1​). Rescaling by (46) gives

dFR ⁣(N(μ0,σ02),N(μ1,σ12))=2 arcosh⁡ ⁣(1+(μ1−μ0)2+2(σ1−σ0)24σ0σ1).\begin{aligned} &d_{\mathrm{FR}}\!\left(N(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2),N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)\right)\\ &\quad=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{arcosh}\!\left( 1+\frac{(\mu_1-\mu_0)^2+2(\sigma_1-\sigma_0)^2} {4\sigma_0\sigma_1}\right). \end{aligned}​dFR​(N(μ0​,σ02​),N(μ1​,σ12​))=2​arcosh(1+4σ0​σ1​(μ1​−μ0​)2+2(σ1​−σ0​)2​).​
(52)

The hyperbolic minimizing-path and distance results used here are treated in Costa–Santos–Strapasson, Fisher information distance: a geometrical reading (2015), §2. Integrating the constant speed in (50) gives the same expression. In particular,

μ0=μ1:dFR=2∣log⁡σ1σ0∣,σ0=σ1=σ:dFR=2 arcosh⁡ ⁣(1+(μ1−μ0)24σ2).\begin{aligned} \mu_0=\mu_1:\quad d_{\mathrm{FR}}&=\sqrt2\left|\log\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0}\right|,\\ \sigma_0=\sigma_1=\sigma:\quad d_{\mathrm{FR}}&=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{arcosh}\!\left( 1+\frac{(\mu_1-\mu_0)^2}{4\sigma^2}\right). \end{aligned}μ0​=μ1​:dFR​σ0​=σ1​=σ:dFR​​=2​∣∣​logσ0​σ1​​∣∣​,=2​arcosh(1+4σ2(μ1​−μ0​)2​).​
(53)

In the fixed-scale one-dimensional subfamily, the distance is instead ∣μ1−μ0∣/σ|\mu_1-\mu_0|/\sigma∣μ1​−μ0​∣/σ. The full-family minimizing path can increase scale while changing location, then decrease it again. For distinct means it is strictly shorter than the horizontal fixed-scale path.

Statistical connections and duality¶

A regular statistical model has more structure than its Fisher metric: third moments of scores distinguish a family of connections. We give their definitions and normal-family calculations here. The duality note develops the resulting Bregman divergence and KL Pythagoras identities.

The cubic tensor and the alpha family¶

Assume sufficient smoothness and integrability to differentiate the Fisher metric, and finite absolute third score moments. Define the Amari–Chentsov cubic tensor by

Cijk=Eξ[sisjsk],C(U,V,W)=CijkUiVjWk.C_{ijk}=\mathbb E_\xi[s_i s_j s_k],\qquad C(U,V,W)=C_{ijk}U^iV^jW^k.Cijk​=Eξ​[si​sj​sk​],C(U,V,W)=Cijk​UiVjWk.
(54)

It is a symmetric covariant tensor because each score transforms as a covector. Raising the last index defines (C♯(U,V))k=gkℓCijℓUiVj(C^\sharp(U,V))^k=g^{k\ell}C_{ij\ell}U^iV^j(C♯(U,V))k=gkℓCijℓ​UiVj.

For α∈R\alpha\in\mathbb Rα∈R, the statistical α\alphaα-connection has coefficients with the output index lowered

Γij,k(α)=Eξ ⁣[(∂i∂jℓξ+1−α2sisj)sk],Γij(α)k=gkℓΓij,ℓ(α).\begin{aligned} \Gamma^{(\alpha)}_{ij,k} &=\mathbb E_\xi\!\left[ \left(\partial_i\partial_j\ell_\xi +\frac{1-\alpha}{2}s_i s_j\right)s_k\right],\\ \Gamma^{(\alpha)k}_{ij}&=g^{k\ell}\Gamma^{(\alpha)}_{ij,\ell}. \end{aligned}Γij,k(α)​Γij(α)k​​=Eξ​[(∂i​∂j​ℓξ​+21−α​si​sj​)sk​],=gkℓΓij,ℓ(α)​.​
(55)

The comma separates the lowered output index; these coefficients themselves are not a covariant tensor. Under a change of chart, the second derivative of ℓ\ellℓ contributes the inhomogeneous term in (36). The coefficients are symmetric in i,ji,ji,j, so all these connections are torsion-free. We use the convention ∇(e)=∇(1)\nabla^{(e)}=\nabla^{(1)}∇(e)=∇(1) and ∇(m)=∇(−1)\nabla^{(m)}=\nabla^{(-1)}∇(m)=∇(−1).

We can identify their relation to Levi-Civita directly. Differentiation of an expectation obeys ∂iEξ[F]=Eξ[∂iF+Fsi]\partial_i\mathbb E_\xi[F]=\mathbb E_\xi[\partial_iF+Fs_i]∂i​Eξ​[F]=Eξ​[∂i​F+Fsi​]. Applying it to gjkg_{jk}gjk​ gives

∂igjk=Eξ[(∂i∂jℓ)sk]+Eξ[sj(∂i∂kℓ)]+Cijk.\partial_i g_{jk} =\mathbb E_\xi[(\partial_i\partial_j\ell)s_k] +\mathbb E_\xi[s_j(\partial_i\partial_k\ell)]+C_{ijk}.∂i​gjk​=Eξ​[(∂i​∂j​ℓ)sk​]+Eξ​[sj​(∂i​∂k​ℓ)]+Cijk​.
(56)

Insert this into the lowered version of the Levi-Civita formula. The mixed terms cancel, leaving

Γij,k(0)=Eξ[(∂i∂jℓ)sk]+12Cijk,∇U(α)V=∇ULCV−α2C♯(U,V).\begin{aligned} \Gamma^{(0)}_{ij,k} &=\mathbb E_\xi[(\partial_i\partial_j\ell)s_k]+\frac12C_{ijk},\\ \nabla^{(\alpha)}_UV &=\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}_UV-\frac\alpha2 C^\sharp(U,V). \end{aligned}Γij,k(0)​∇U(α)​V​=Eξ​[(∂i​∂j​ℓ)sk​]+21​Cijk​,=∇ULC​V−2α​C♯(U,V).​
(57)

This proves that the α=0\alpha=0α=0 connection is Levi-Civita and expresses the difference of connections as a tensor.

Dual connections¶

Two connections ∇\nabla∇ and ∇∗\nabla^*∇∗ are dual with respect to ggg when

U[g(V,W)]=g(∇UV,W)+g(V,∇U∗W).U[g(V,W)]=g(\nabla_UV,W)+g(V,\nabla^*_UW).U[g(V,W)]=g(∇U​V,W)+g(V,∇U∗​W).
(58)

Substitute (57) on the right, once with α\alphaα and once with −α-\alpha−α. The cubic terms cancel by symmetry, and Levi-Civita compatibility supplies the left side. Thus ∇(α)\nabla^{(\alpha)}∇(α) and ∇(−α)\nabla^{(-\alpha)}∇(−α) are dual, including the e/m pair. If VVV is parallel for one connection and WWW for its dual along the same curve, g(V,W)g(V,W)g(V,W) is constant. Neither transport separately needs to preserve g(V,V)g(V,V)g(V,V). Indeed, (∇U(α)g)(V,W)=αC(U,V,W)(\nabla^{(\alpha)}_U g)(V,W)=\alpha C(U,V,W)(∇U(α)​g)(V,W)=αC(U,V,W), so nonzero α\alphaα generally breaks metric compatibility.

These definitions and the sign convention agree with Amari and Nagaoka, Methods of Information Geometry (2000) and Amari, Information Geometry and Its Applications (2016). The calculations above establish the displayed relations under the stated regularity assumptions.

The normal alpha-connections¶

Natural and expectation coordinates make different connections flat¶

In the natural chart, ∂i∂jℓθ=−∂i∂jψ\partial_i\partial_j\ell_\theta=-\partial_i\partial_j\psi∂i​∂j​ℓθ​=−∂i​∂j​ψ is independent of the observation. Since every score has expectation zero, (55) at α=1\alpha=1α=1 gives Γij(e)k=0\Gamma^{(e)k}_{ij}=0Γij(e)k​=0. Also Cijk=∂i∂j∂kψC_{ijk}=\partial_i\partial_j\partial_k\psiCijk​=∂i​∂j​∂k​ψ in these coordinates, by differentiating the covariance of t(X)t(X)t(X).

The expectation chart makes the dual mixture coefficients vanish. Here is a coordinate argument. The natural coordinate vector fields Ei=∂/∂θiE_i=\partial/\partial\theta^iEi​=∂/∂θi are e-parallel. Let Fa=∂/∂ηaF_a=\partial/\partial\eta^aFa​=∂/∂ηa. Since dθ=Gθ−1dηd\theta=G_\theta^{-1}d\etadθ=Gθ−1​dη,

g(Ei,Fa)=∑j(Gθ)ij(Gθ−1)ja={1,i=a,0,i≠a.g(E_i,F_a) =\sum_j (G_\theta)_{ij}(G_\theta^{-1})_{ja} =\begin{cases}1,&i=a,\\0,&i\ne a.\end{cases}g(Ei​,Fa​)=j∑​(Gθ​)ij​(Gθ−1​)ja​={1,0,​i=a,i=a.​
(63)

The explicit sum here multiplies matrices labeled by two different coordinate bases; the numeric identity compares their paired labels. Differentiate this constant pairing with any field UUU and use e/m duality. Because ∇U(e)Ei=0\nabla^{(e)}_UE_i=0∇U(e)​Ei​=0, we obtain g(Ei,∇U(m)Fa)=0g(E_i,\nabla^{(m)}_UF_a)=0g(Ei​,∇U(m)​Fa​)=0 for every iii, hence ∇U(m)Fa=0\nabla^{(m)}_UF_a=0∇U(m)​Fa​=0. In particular, all m-Christoffel symbols vanish in the η\etaη chart.

Both connections therefore have zero curvature. This dual flatness coexists with the curvature −1/2-1/2−1/2 of ∇LC\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}∇LC. Curvature is attached to a specified connection; the vanishing of the e- or m-coefficients in their affine charts does not make the Fisher metric Euclidean.

Three geodesics between two normal laws¶

Let P0=N(μ0,σ02)P_0=N(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2)P0​=N(μ0​,σ02​) and P1=N(μ1,σ12)P_1=N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)P1​=N(μ1​,σ12​) with positive scales, and let 0≤r≤10\leq r\leq10≤r≤1. A straight natural-coordinate segment is an affinely parameterized e-geodesic. In location-scale coordinates it is

θ(r)=(1−r)θ0+rθ1,σe2(r)=(1−rσ02+rσ12)−1,μe(r)=σe2(r)((1−r)μ0σ02+rμ1σ12).\begin{aligned} \theta(r)&=(1-r)\theta_0+r\theta_1,\\ \sigma_e^2(r)&=\left(\frac{1-r}{\sigma_0^2} +\frac r{\sigma_1^2}\right)^{-1},\\ \mu_e(r)&=\sigma_e^2(r) \left(\frac{(1-r)\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2} +\frac{r\mu_1}{\sigma_1^2}\right). \end{aligned}θ(r)σe2​(r)μe​(r)​=(1−r)θ0​+rθ1​,=(σ02​1−r​+σ12​r​)−1,=σe2​(r)(σ02​(1−r)μ0​​+σ12​rμ1​​).​
(64)

It interpolates precision and precision-weighted mean. Its density is proportional to p01−rp1rp_0^{1-r}p_1^rp01−r​p1r​, as follows by interpolating the natural form. The precision stays positive, so the whole segment belongs to the family.

A straight expectation-coordinate segment is an affinely parameterized m-geodesic of the connection on this normal family:

η(r)=(1−r)η0+rη1,μm(r)=(1−r)μ0+rμ1,σm2(r)=(1−r)σ02+rσ12+r(1−r)(μ1−μ0)2.\begin{aligned} \eta(r)&=(1-r)\eta_0+r\eta_1,\\ \mu_m(r)&=(1-r)\mu_0+r\mu_1,\\ \sigma_m^2(r)&=(1-r)\sigma_0^2+r\sigma_1^2 +r(1-r)(\mu_1-\mu_0)^2. \end{aligned}η(r)μm​(r)σm2​(r)​=(1−r)η0​+rη1​,=(1−r)μ0​+rμ1​,=(1−r)σ02​+rσ12​+r(1−r)(μ1​−μ0​)2.​
(65)

The last term follows by subtracting the square of the interpolated mean from the interpolated second raw moment. It keeps variance positive. This normal has the same first two moments as (1−r)P0+rP1(1-r)P_0+rP_1(1−r)P0​+rP1​, but is generally not that literal mixture: a mixture of two distinct normals need not be normal. Thus m-flatness of this family does not assert closure under density mixtures. Differentiating the two displayed paths verifies (61) at α=1\alpha=1α=1 and α=−1\alpha=-1α=−1 respectively.

For comparison, the Levi-Civita segment is the vertical path or half-ellipse in (50), with endpoints chosen as above. It minimizes Fisher length; e- and m-geodesics are straight for their respective connections and have no general Fisher-length-minimization property.

For P0=N(0,1)P_0=N(0,1)P0​=N(0,1) and P1=N(2,1)P_1=N(2,1)P1​=N(2,1) the difference is explicit:

m, α=−1\alpha=-1α=−1μ=2r\mu=2rμ=2r, σ2=1+4r(1−r)\sigma^2=1+4r(1-r)σ2=1+4r(1−r)2\sqrt22​

The Levi-Civita parameter in this comparison is the affine hyperbolic parameter, not generally μ/2\mu/2μ/2. Its length is 2 arcosh⁡(2)\sqrt2\,\operatorname{arcosh}(2)2​arcosh(2); the horizontal e-path has length 2. If the endpoints have equal means, all three paths trace the same vertical segment, but their affine parameterizations generally differ: e interpolates precision, m interpolates variance, and Levi-Civita interpolates log scale.

Continue with exponential families for sufficient statistics and the log-partition function, or dual coordinates and KL projections for the Bregman and Pythagorean consequences. The Information Geometry hub lists the complete entry path.
